concept.centerRule: A Scene belongs when a bounded source materially states or narratively establishes a relation between action, condition, allegiance, speech, or prior event and a named outcome. Shared vocabulary never erases speaker, agency, timing, reach, reversal, exception, or uncertainty.

characterAnchors.label: Adam
characterAnchors.note: Acts in Genesis 3 and later anchors Paul’s one-and-many consequence argument.

characterAnchors.label: Cain
characterAnchors.note: Receives curse, fear, protection, and continuing life after murdering Abel.

characterAnchors.label: Abraham
characterAnchors.note: Questions collective judgment and later receives blessing language tied to his action.

characterAnchors.label: Joseph
characterAnchors.note: Distinguishes his brothers’ harmful intention from a life-preserving outcome.

characterAnchors.label: Moses
characterAnchors.note: Mediates covenant warnings, intercession, wilderness judgment, and the appeal to choose life.

characterAnchors.label: Saul
characterAnchors.note: Explains his action while Samuel connects rejected command to rejected kingship.

characterAnchors.label: David
characterAnchors.note: Receives forgiveness while household and public consequences remain named.

characterAnchors.label: Job
characterAnchors.note: Suffers losses not attributed to guilt and later becomes the intercessor for rejected explanations.

characterAnchors.label: Jesus Christ
characterAnchors.note: Teaches about fruit and response while rejecting simple guilt explanations for suffering.

characterAnchors.label: Paul
characterAnchors.note: Distinguishes deeds, one-and-many agency, wages and gift, discipline, sowing, reaping, and future judgment.

concept.throughline: The trail moves from actions and family outcomes through covenant consequence, rulers and exile, wisdom’s challenges to simple formulas, prophetic accusation, Jesus’ teaching, assembly life, and final judgment and access.

edges.basis: Both narratives join grave human action to divine judgment while preserving clothing, protection, and life beyond the immediate sentence. The eating, questioning, accusations, judgments, altered labor and relationships, mortality, clothing, and expulsion are narrated in one consequence sequence. Cain’s anger, murder, questioning, curse, fear, protection, and departure distinguish deed, judgment, mercy, and ongoing life.
edges.label: Eating leads into altered life and expulsion · Cain receives judgment and protection after murder

edges.basis: Genesis presents two communal outcomes with different triggers, reach, and forms of preservation. Human violence and corruption are named before flood judgment, while Noah’s favor and obedience shape another outcome. The city and tower project ends in confused language and scattering, and the place-name remembers the stated relation.
edges.label: Violence, flood judgment, favor, and obedience · The tower project ends in confused language and scattering

edges.basis: Abraham disputes the reach of one judgment and later receives a blessing tied to his own action. The announced investigation of Sodom opens a dispute about collective judgment, righteous people, and the reach of consequence. The angel relates Abraham’s action to blessing language after the commanded sacrifice has been halted.
edges.label: Abraham questions the reach of Sodom’s judgment · Abraham’s action is followed by renewed blessing

edges.basis: Jacob’s deception and the brothers’ deception both fracture a household while their later paths diverge. Jacob’s deception produces blessing, Esau’s hostility, Rebekah’s plan, and separation whose length she cannot know. Joseph’s brothers’ plot leads through violence, sale, deception, grief, and an outcome in Egypt they do not yet understand.
edges.label: Deception produces blessing, hostility, and separation · The brothers’ plot carries Joseph into Egypt

edges.basis: The scenes distinguish human intent, divine purpose, royal command, refusal, and outcomes none of the human actors fully commands. Joseph distinguishes his brothers’ intended harm from God’s intended life-preserving outcome without erasing their action. The midwives fear God, refuse the king’s command, answer Pharaoh, receive households, and face a new royal decree.
edges.label: Human evil intention and life-preserving outcome remain together · The midwives refuse Pharaoh and receive households

edges.basis: Both Exodus scenes place judgment beside mediated protection, yet their agents, households, and remaining consequences differ. Passover action, protection, death, outcry, release, and demanded departure unfold with different household outcomes. The calf episode moves through disorder, Levite violence, intercession, threatened erasure, and plague without one simple outcome.
edges.label: Passover divides household outcomes and forces release · The calf brings violence, intercession, and plague

edges.basis: One legal sequence explicitly provides confession and covenant remembrance; the wilderness narrative portrays a late attempt that ignores the stated command. Obedience and refusal are followed through escalating blessing, curse, exile, confession, remembrance, and covenant mercy. The wilderness generation’s refusal leads to delayed entry, forty years, attempted reversal, and defeat.
edges.label: Covenant consequence includes escalation and remembrance · Refusal leads to wandering, attempted reversal, and defeat

edges.basis: Both wilderness crises name leadership action and communal consequence without giving every participant the same role. Korah’s challenge produces several judgments, continuing complaint, plague, intercession, and a halted outcome. Moses and Aaron’s action at Meribah is followed by a stated loss of entry and the naming of the disputed waters.
edges.label: Korah’s challenge continues through complaint and plague · Meribah is followed by lost entry

edges.basis: One narrative reports an immediate plague and covenant claim; one speech warns a future settled generation about pride and forgetting. Israel’s attachment at Peor leads to anger, plague, violent intervention, halted judgment, and a covenant claim. Land, abundance, memory, pride, forgetting, and destruction are linked in a warning about future consequence.
edges.label: Peor leads to plague, intervention, and covenant · Abundance creates a warning about pride and forgetting

edges.basis: The long national catalogue and the closing personal-communal appeal address outcome at different scales. Blessings and curses expand obedience and refusal into bodily, economic, military, political, land, and exile outcomes. Life and death, blessing and curse, choice, love, obedience, clinging, and land are placed before Israel.
edges.label: Blessing and curse reach body, land, rule, and exile · Life and death are placed before Israel

edges.basis: The sources attribute communal trouble to materially different patterns: a concealed taking and a recurring generational relapse. Achan’s hidden taking is connected to Israel’s defeat, investigation, confession, judgment, and restored anger. Israel’s repeated abandonment is narrated through anger, oppression, crying, judges, relief, relapse, and retained nations.
edges.label: A hidden taking becomes public defeat and judgment · Abandonment, oppression, relief, and relapse repeat

edges.basis: Narrator requital and prophetic household judgment each extend consequence beyond an isolated private act. Abimelech and Shechem’s violence returns through conflict and death, and the narrator explicitly names requital. Priestly contempt and Eli’s household are addressed through a rejected promise, deaths, loss of office, and a surviving dependent.
edges.label: Abimelech and Shechem’s violence returns upon them · Eli’s household loses a promised priestly future

edges.basis: Both kings receive prophetic confrontation, but forgiveness, office, household consequence, and future rule do not align in the same way. Saul’s rejection of the command is connected to rejection as king while grief and the LORD’s regret remain in view. Nathan’s accusation connects David’s taking and killing to death, household violence, public exposure, forgiveness, and another child.
edges.label: Saul’s rejected command becomes rejected kingship · David is forgiven while household consequences remain

edges.basis: One delay is stated for David’s sake; the other follows Ahab’s humility, preserving distinct grounds and reach. Solomon’s attachments and worship are followed by divine anger and a kingdom division delayed for David’s sake. Ahab’s seizure of Naboth’s vineyard receives a judgment oracle that is delayed after humility.
edges.label: Solomon’s kingdom judgment is delayed and limited · Ahab’s humility delays announced disaster

edges.basis: One source explains a kingdom’s exile; another narrates one king’s divided life after unauthorized sanctuary action. Samaria’s fall is interpreted through a long account of worship, refusal, prophetic warning, exile, and covenant breach. Uzziah’s strength leads to pride, unauthorized sanctuary action, skin disease, exclusion, and a divided royal life.
edges.label: Samaria’s exile receives a long explanation · Strength turns to pride, intrusion, and exclusion

edges.basis: The postexilic prayers preserve remnant mercy without denying renewed failure or foreign rule. Ezra reads exile and fragile restoration through accumulated guilt, mercy, remnant, and renewed unfaithfulness. The prayer traces rebellion, consequence, mercy, repeated relapse, foreign rule, and present distress.
edges.label: Ezra reads renewed failure inside fragile mercy · A prayer traces rebellion, mercy, and present distress

edges.basis: The narrator identifies Job as blameless while Eliphaz later presents a general guilt-and-suffering rule. Job’s losses are not attributed to his wrongdoing, challenging the friends’ later consequence assumptions. Eliphaz argues that people reap what they plow, presenting a consequence claim the book later subjects to scrutiny.
edges.label: Job loses everything without a guilt explanation · Eliphaz claims people reap what they plow

edges.basis: Job judges an attempted application to one sufferer; Psalm 1 remains a poetic portrait rather than a complete case history. The LORD rejects the friends’ speech, requires Job’s prayer, restores Job, and leaves several causal questions unanswered. Two ways are pictured through rooted fruitfulness, chaff, judgment, divine knowledge, and perishing.
edges.label: The friends are rebuked and Job is restored · Two ways end in fruitfulness and chaff

edges.basis: Both poems refuse envy while taking present prosperity seriously and locating judgment beyond the immediate view. The psalm contrasts short-lived wrongdoing, patient trust, inherited land, observed endings, and deliverance. The speaker’s envy at wicked prosperity changes after sanctuary insight into their end and his own nearness to God.
edges.label: Patient trust looks beyond short-lived wrongdoing · Wicked prosperity unsettles the speaker until sanctuary insight

edges.basis: Fruit, pursuit, generosity, complacency, and trouble appear as wisdom observations whose literary form matters. Rejected wisdom is followed by calamity, self-produced fruit, complacency, and a contrasting secure hearing. Work, pursuit, generosity, withholding, trust, fruit, trouble, and recompense form clustered consequence observations.
edges.label: Rejected wisdom leads to eating one’s own fruit · Pursuit, generosity, trust, and trouble carry outcomes

edges.basis: Proverbs supplies compact results; Ecclesiastes foregrounds delay, injustice, and limits on human knowledge. Humility, fear, diligence, debt, oppression, generosity, and named results are placed in short observations. Delayed sentence, repeated wrongdoing, claimed outcomes, observed injustice, and unknowable divine work resist simple formulas.
edges.label: Humility, debt, generosity, and oppression receive named results · Delayed sentence complicates moral prediction

edges.basis: One source limits predictable moral inference; the other explicitly interprets one prophetic vineyard and its public judgment. The same event reaches righteous and wicked, while time and chance challenge predictable outcome claims. The vineyard’s failed fruit is connected to removal, devastation, injustice oracles, and invading judgment.
edges.label: One event, time, and chance reach different people · Failed vineyard fruit leads into public devastation

edges.basis: The prophetic sources distinguish divine use, human boasting, injustice, false security, and judgment. Assyria acts as an instrument yet boasts as autonomous, and judgment turns against the instrument’s arrogance. Temple confidence, injustice, false worship, prophetic warning, Shiloh memory, and poured-out anger are connected.
edges.label: The instrument boasts and becomes the object of judgment · Temple confidence cannot shield injustice

edges.basis: Both sources confront intergenerational shorthand while developing individual action, reversal, forgiveness, and future covenant. Sowing, rebuilding, individual responsibility language, new covenant, forgiveness, and remembered sin are held together. A disputed proverb about parents and children is answered through individual conduct, reversibility, judgment, and a call to turn.
edges.label: Sowing, responsibility, and new covenant belong to restoration · Ezekiel rejects inherited-guilt shorthand

edges.basis: Ezekiel explicitly allows changed conduct to change the stated outcome; Hosea names a people’s continuing allegiance and harvest. Despair over accumulated sin is answered through turning, changed conduct, watchman warning, and individual judgment. Israel sows wind and reaps whirlwind as rejected allegiance, kingship, idolatry, failed grain, and exile converge.
edges.label: Despair is answered by turning and responsibility · Israel sows wind and reaps whirlwind

edges.basis: Each prophet supplies a source-specific interpretation that cannot be generalized to every disaster or public collapse. A sequence of disasters is repeatedly followed by “yet you haven’t returned,” ending in an unresolved summons. Rulers, prophets, priests, violence, paid speech, false security, unanswered cries, and Zion’s ruin are linked.
edges.label: Repeated disasters fail to produce return · Violent leadership ends in unanswered cries and ruin

edges.basis: The taunt songs portray violence returning; Malachi promises a future distinction amid present dispute. The taunt sayings return plunder, violence, shame, and idolatry upon the one who built by them. The dispute over serving God asks what result follows faithfulness and ends with a promised distinction not yet visible.
edges.label: The taunts return plunder, violence, and shame · A disputed result awaits a future distinction

edges.basis: The sources retain human alliance and violence alongside a narrator claim about the devil without reducing one to the other. Death is related to human pursuit and alliance while God is denied as its author in the surrounding argument. The plot against the righteous and the claim about death through the devil expose speaker action and narrator interpretation.
edges.label: Wisdom denies God as death’s author and names human pursuit · A human plot and a narrator’s claim about death

edges.basis: Both sources interpret suffering through faithfulness and future hope while preserving different speakers and historical scenes. Apparent death and punishment are contrasted with hope, tested faithfulness, rule, and the fruitlessness of the ungodly. Children, presumption, mercy, wrath, hiddenness, and creation are used to challenge confidence that actions escape notice.
edges.label: Apparent punishment is contrasted with tested hope · Presumption that deeds go unnoticed is challenged

edges.basis: One narrative records contested testimony under torture; one teaching discourse connects hearing and doing to future outcome. The brothers interpret torture, death, resurrection, discipline, and the persecutor’s future within contested speech. Two roads, fruit, confession, obedience, foundations, storm, collapse, endurance, and authority frame stated outcomes.
edges.label: Martyrs interpret suffering through discipline and resurrection · Roads, fruit, confession, and foundations disclose outcomes

edges.basis: One parable follows reception under pressure and distraction; the other follows received mercy into refused mercy. The sower parable and explanation distinguish hearing, resistance, pressure, distraction, reception, and varied fruit. Received mercy, refused mercy, restored debt, punishment, and Jesus’ concluding warning form a consequence parable.
edges.label: Hearing produces different outcomes across the soils · Received mercy is followed by refused mercy and punishment

edges.basis: Delay and hidden growth create different tests of response, fear, measure, desire, and fruit. Entrusted resources, delay, action, fear, accounting, service, neglect, judgment, and differing outcomes are narrated. Hearing, concealment, measure, possession, soils, pressure, desire, and fruit are connected within the parable discourse.
edges.label: Delay exposes different responses to entrusted resources · Hearing, measure, pressure, and fruit remain connected

edges.basis: Both Lukan sources join abundance to death while differing in narrator frame, neighbor visibility, reversal, and warning evidence. Greed, abundance, planned ease, sudden death, treasure, anxiety, giving, and the heart’s location are juxtaposed. The rich man and Lazarus undergo reversed outcomes while memory, chasm, Moses, prophets, and persuasion remain central.
edges.label: Abundance and planned ease meet sudden death · Death reverses two lives and fixes a chasm

edges.basis: John 3 describes people approaching or avoiding light; John 9 rejects a direct sin-to-disability inference and follows testimony. Belief, unbelief, life, judgment, love of darkness, evil action, truth, and coming to light receive explicit relations. Jesus rejects a simple sin-to-blindness inference, heals the man, and turns the scene toward testimony and claimed sight.
edges.label: Belief and unbelief are shown through action toward light · Jesus rejects the proposed cause of blindness

edges.basis: Jesus’ vine discourse develops enduring relationship and fruit; Acts narrates one severe communal deception outcome. Abiding, pruning, word, prayer, fruit, love, obedience, friendship, and lasting appointment are related without one simple mechanism. Property freedom, deception, confrontation, deaths, burial, and great fear form a severe communal outcome scene.
edges.label: Abiding, pruning, fruit, prayer, and love remain distinct · A voluntary property decision becomes deception, death, and fear

edges.basis: Both scenes concern public responses to power and the word, but their human actions and community outcomes differ. Herod receives acclaim, is struck, dies, and is contrasted with the growing word of God. Extraordinary works, failed imitation, fear, confession, costly renunciation, and growth of the word unfold together.
edges.label: Herod receives acclaim, dies, and is contrasted with the word · Failed imitation leads to fear, confession, and costly renunciation

edges.basis: Romans moves from a broad account of exchanged worship to direct scrutiny of the judging reader. Suppressed truth, exchanged worship, repeated divine handing-over, conduct, knowledge, and approval form a consequence argument. Judgment of others, persistence, hardening, deeds, conscience, law, and impartial judgment are connected.
edges.label: Exchanged worship is followed by repeated handing over · Judging others does not escape impartial judgment

edges.basis: The adjacent arguments use different causal, representative, slavery, fruit, wages, and gift vocabularies. Adam and Christ anchor an argument about one act, many people, death, condemnation, obedience, grace, and life. Obedience, slavery, fruit, shame, holiness, death as wages, and life as gift are distinguished.
edges.label: Adam and Christ anchor different one-and-many outcomes · Fruit, shame, wages, and gift are not interchangeable

edges.basis: Romans refuses to erase suffering; Corinthians distinguishes the worker, God’s growth, the foundation, tested work, reward, and loss. Present suffering, creation’s frustration, hope, Spirit-aided weakness, providence, accusation, and inseparable love are held together. Planting, watering, growth, foundation, building quality, fire, reward, loss, and Temple destruction receive distinct agencies.
edges.label: Suffering, hope, providence, accusation, and love · Growth and tested work receive different agencies

edges.basis: Paul names present weakness and discipline in Corinth while separately describing universal appearance before Christ. Division, unequal eating, remembrance, self-examination, weakness, sickness, deaths, discipline, and condemnation are connected. Mortality, Spirit, courage, pleasing Christ, and appearing for deeds done in the body shape future consequence.
edges.label: Meal inequality is connected to weakness and discipline · Mortality and the Spirit lead toward appearing for deeds

edges.basis: One argument centers community restoration and perseverance; the other contrasts named conduct, deception, wrath, and wise walking. Restoration, burden, self-testing, teaching support, sowing, reaping, perseverance, and doing good are joined. Love, self-giving, named conduct, inheritance, deception, wrath, light, exposed fruit, and wise walking are contrasted.
edges.label: Restoration and burden-bearing frame sowing and reaping · Named conduct, wrath, light, and fruit contrast two walks

edges.basis: Colossians addresses household service and repayment; James distinguishes human desire from God’s good giving. Household duties, service to the Lord Christ, inheritance, and impartial repayment are placed together. Testing, desire, sin, death, divine gifts, implanted word, doing, speech, care, and unstained life form a sequence.
edges.label: Household service is addressed through inheritance and repayment · Desire gives birth to sin while God gives good gifts

edges.basis: The letter connects speech to fire and disorder, then wealth and withheld wages to judgment, patience, and repair. Teaching responsibility, speech, bodily direction, destructive fire, inconsistent blessing, wisdom, peace, and righteous fruit are related. Stored wealth, withheld wages, luxury, judgment, patience, prayer, sickness, confession, restoration, and rescue from death appear together.
edges.label: Speech can destroy while peace sows righteous fruit · Withheld wages, patience, prayer, and rescue share a warning

edges.basis: Peter distinguishes blessed conduct from present suffering, delayed destruction, rescue, and corrupt return. Retaliation and blessing, guarded speech, doing good, divine attention, suffering, and a defense of hope are distinguished. False teaching, exploitation, delayed destruction, past judgments, rescue, corruption, and return to former conduct are connected.
edges.label: Retaliation and blessing lead into suffering for good · Delayed destruction stands beside rescue and return to corruption

edges.basis: One letter explains apparent delay through patience; Revelation’s messages retain urgent, community-specific consequences. Apparent delay, patience, repentance, coming judgment, holy conduct, expectation, instability, and growth frame the future. The assemblies receive distinct praise, accusation, commands, warnings, promises, and consequences for hearing or refusing.
edges.label: Apparent delay is interpreted as patience · Each assembly receives a distinct warning and promise

edges.basis: Revelation retains deeds, books, access, exclusion, testimony, coming, and grace without fully explaining every relation. The dead are judged according to deeds, death and Hades are removed, and the book of life marks a final boundary. Continuing conduct, recompense, access, exclusion, testimony, alteration warnings, promised coming, and grace close the canon.
edges.label: Judgment according to deeds stands beside the book of life · Recompense, access, exclusion, testimony, and grace close the canon
